items.summary: Every insolvency tribunal hears the same line from counsel for the corporate debtor: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) is not a recovery mechanism. Yet, ask the supplier who files under Section 9 why he has come and the honest answer is almost always the same: he wants to be paid. If resolution is the Code’s only legitimate purpose, does the law give the operational creditor any reason to want it? And why may he start a process in which he can lawfully be left with next to nothing? This piece argues that demanding a “resolution motive” from him is largely a fiction, which the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 has not cured. The better question is whether the debtor needs a collective process and whether the creditor can be given a fair route to payment before one begins. items.title: Adivasi children in Maharashtra are dying of malnutrition. What’s the state doing?
items.summary: On January 30, Ajit Kasdekar died. He was two years old. Ajit was afflicted with severe wasting (loss of muscle fat and tissue) and acute malnutrition. According to growth charts released by the government, Ajit should have weighed 12 kg. He was just four kg when he was admitted to the nutritional rehabilitation centre of the Dharni sub-district hospital in November. When he died, he weighed six kg. Ajit’s mother, Sharmila, 22, is a Korku Adivasi from Berdabarda village in Dharni taluka of Amravati, Maharashtra. “I don’t understand, it happened all of a sudden. We were happy that he had gained some weight,” she said. “He had developed a small ulcer in his mouth and was a little fatigued when we brought him back from the hospital on the evening of January 30. He ate only a small portion of cooked rice, like he always does, for dinner and slept. It was hard for us to see him not waking up from his sleep the next morning.” The immediate and exact cause of Ajit’s death is not known since Sharmila didn’t take him back to the hospital. items.title: The curious case of protesters’ missing phones: Neither FIR for ‘snatching’, nor memo for ‘seizure’
items.summary: Amid the recent protests and thousands of detentions in Delhi, at least 24 mobile phones belonging to detainees remain unaccounted for. Their owners were detained around 4 pm on October 11 in Connaught Place. A complaint was sent to the police accusing four policemen of snatching the phones the same day. But lawyers who helped the detainees filed the complaint claimed the police refused to register a regular FIR. They say they were compelled to opt for an e-FIR – lodged on October 16 at the Connaught Place police station on theft charges despite the alleged snatching. Connaught Place police station SHO Sukhbir Malik denied the allegations and said the police are probing the matter. “We did not take anyone’s phones. Justice M Nagaprasanna observed that a parent who knowingly allows a minor to drive cannot automatically escape criminal liability when the act ends in tragedy. The Court held that the prosecution must be allowed to proceed against accused man, Nadeem Ur Rehman, as the chargesheet contained prima facie material indicating that he had handed over the car keys to his minor son and permitted him to drive. "A parent who knowingly places the steering wheel in the hands of a child cannot always retreat behind the minority of that child, when the adventure ends in catastrophe. Parenthood carries not merely affection and authority, but responsibility. Roads are shared public spaces, not training grounds for unlawful indulgence," the Court held.
